Complete Empirical Research Plan

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study in a region-year panel.

Rationale  
• The 1991 liberalization is a nationwide “event,” but the magnitude of the tariff cut differed sharply across industries.  
• Regions (states or districts) differed in their pre-1991 industry mix. A region that employed many workers in industries whose tariffs fell a lot experienced a larger “treatment dose.”  
• These differences are predetermined (based on the 1987–88 NSS employment structure) and are therefore plausibly exogenous to post-1991 poverty changes, satisfying the DID requirement of conditionally parallel trends.  
• An event-study (year-by-year coefficients relative to 1991) tests the parallel-trends assumption and illustrates dynamics.  
• Heterogeneity in factor immobility enters as a third difference: regions with low labor mobility should be more affected.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
TradeShock_r  ≡  Σ_i  (EmploymentShare_{ri,1987}  ×  ΔTariff_i)  
ΔTariff_i = (Tariff_i, pre-1991) – (Tariff_i, post-1991 average 1992–2000).  
A larger (more negative) TradeShock_r means a larger tariff decline, i.e. heavier exposure.

Control Group / Counterfactual  
Regions whose initial industry mix made them minimally exposed (e.g., bottom quartile of |TradeShock_r|) act as controls. In the continuous specification they still enter; identification comes from relative differences in exposure.

Treatment Timing  
Post_t = 1 for survey rounds 1993–94, 1995–96, 1999–00; 0 for 1987–88, 1989–90, 1991 NSS rounds. 1991 is coded as pre-period because implementation lags.

No RDD applies; there is no running variable with a known cutoff.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of liberalization, poverty in high- and low-exposure regions would have followed similar trends.  
Plausibility: Industrial composition in 1987 precedes the reform; pre-trend tests with 1987–91 data can assess it.

A2. Exogeneity of Pre-reform Industry Mix: 1987 industrial structure is unrelated to future idiosyncratic poverty shocks.  
Institutional support: Industry mix was shaped by decades of license-permit policies, not by anticipations of 1991 reforms.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Cross-region Spillovers): One region’s tariff shock does not directly change another region’s poverty (except through aggregate macro channels captured by year effects).  
Plausibility: Internal migration was limited; still, we will test for migration-related spillovers.

A4. No Simultaneous Policy Shocks Correlated with Treatment Intensity: Other reforms (e.g., financial sector or investment-license delicensing) are not differentially correlated with TradeShock_r.  
Plausibility: Will control for exposure to other reforms using similar shift-share constructs.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Pre-trends  
• Mitigation: (i) Event-study coefficients for 1987, 1989, 1991 must be statistically zero. (ii) Include state-specific linear pre-trends.

T2. Selective Migration (endogenous mobility)  
• Mitigation: (i) Compute region-level net-migration rates and control for them. (ii) Repeat main regressions on subsample of households present in the same region in two consecutive rounds (panel subset). (iii) Use factor-immobility measure only from pre-1991 migration records to avoid mechanical correlation.

T3. Concurrent Reforms Correlated with Industry Mix  
• Mitigation: Create similar shift-share variables for delicensing (industrial licensing abolition) and financial-sector deregulation; control for them simultaneously.  
• Robustness: Drop highly regulated industries as of 1990.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# -------------------------------------------------
# Household data (NSS rounds pooled)
hh  <- fread("NSS_household_1987_2000.csv")      # household-level
# Industry-level tariff series
tar <- fread("tariffs_1980_2000.csv")            # HS/ISIC codes, ad-valorem rates
# Region-industry employment (1987)
emp <- fread("employmentShares_1987.csv")        # region, industry, share

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------------
# 2a. Construct industry-level tariff fall  (pre minus post)
tar_pre  <- tar[year==1990,  .(industry, tariff_pre = tariff)]
tar_post <- tar[year>=1992 & year<=2000,
                .(tariff_post = mean(tariff)), by = industry]
dTar <- merge(tar_pre, tar_post, by="industry")
dTar[, delta_tariff := tariff_pre - tariff_post]  # positive if tariff went down

# 2b. Region-level TradeShock (shift-share)
shock <- merge(emp, dTar, by="industry")
shock[, contrib := share * delta_tariff]
shock_r <- shock[, .(TradeShock = sum(contrib)), by = region]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2c. Merge shock with household data
# -------------------------------------------------
hh <- merge(hh, shock_r, by="region", all.x = TRUE)

# 2d. Post indicator
hh[, post := (year >= 1993)]

# 2e. Outcome
hh[, poor := as.integer(cons_real < poverty_line)]        # poverty headcount

# 2f. Labor immobility proxy (pre-1991 net migration * −1)
imm <- fread("migration_1981_1991.csv")                   # region-level
hh  <- merge(hh, imm, by="region", all.x=TRUE)
hh[, low_mob := as.integer(net_migration_rate < quantile(net_migration_rate,.25))]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Specification
# -------------------------------------------------
# Region & year fixed effects
est_main <- feols(poor ~ TradeShock*post | region + year, data = hh,
                  cluster = ~region)
summary(est_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Triple-difference (heterogeneity by immobility)
# -------------------------------------------------
est_het <- feols(poor ~ TradeShock*post*low_mob | region + year, data = hh,
                 cluster = ~region)
summary(est_het)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Event-study
# -------------------------------------------------
hh[, rel_year := year - 1991]
event <- feols(poor ~ i(rel_year, TradeShock, ref = -1) | region + year,
               data = hh, cluster = ~region)
iplot(event)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: placebo tariff changes 1980-1986
# -------------------------------------------------
# Build placebo shock using 1980-86 tariff changes
dTar_placebo <- tar[year==1980,.(industry,tar80=tariff)][tar[year==1986,.(industry,tar86=tariff)],
                      on="industry"][,delta80_86:= tar80 - tar86]
shock_pl <- merge(emp, dTar_placebo, by="industry")
shock_pl[, contrib:= share*delta80_86]
shock_pl_r <- shock_pl[,.(PlaceboShock = sum(contrib)), by=region]
hh <- merge(hh, shock_pl_r, by="region", all.x=TRUE)

est_placebo <- feols(poor ~ PlaceboShock*post | region + year, data=hh, cluster = ~region)
summary(est_placebo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests import-competition may hurt poor households in immobile regions through wage declines and sectoral dislocation.  
Prior: A one-standard-deviation larger tariff fall (≈ 20 percentage points) increases the poverty headcount ratio by about 2–3 percentage points in low-mobility regions, and close to zero in high-mobility regions. We also expect the negative effect to fade after 6–8 years as labor re-allocates.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically confirmed…..   1  
C2: No anticipation or manipulation around policy change…….   1  
C3: No time-varying confounders correlated with treatment….   0.5 (other reforms)  
C4: No spillovers across units………………………………………   0.5  
C5: Correct inference (clustered, serial corr.)………………   1  

Total = 4.0 / 5  

-------------------------------------------------
End of plan
